The 33-year-old Spaniard won Saturday's sprint race and would have clinched a second successive title, drawing level with Valentino Rossi's record tally, had main rival Jorge Martin finished outside the points in Sunday's grand prix. However, Martin - the 2024 champion - returned from injury after withdrawing from the previous race with a fractured wrist to finish seventh. Ducatti rider Marquez has a 60-point lead over Aprilia's Martin and will have another chance to clinch the title in the season's penultimate race weekend in Portimao, Portugal, in two weeks' time. Pole-sitter Bezzecchi, Martin's Aprilia team-mate, claimed his sixth grand prix win of the season, while Spain's Trackhouse Aprilia rider Raul Fernandez was third. stories.title: It's not 'colonialism', it's 'invasion': Burkina Faso corrects Africa's history
stories.description: The government subsequently distributed a 190-page guide to teachers to support implementation, pending the production of revised textbooks.
stories.excerpt: Burkina Faso has introduced sweeping changes to its school curriculum under President Ibrahim Traoré, replacing colonial-era terminology and adding lessons intended to strengthen African identity, patriotism and national pride. The reforms, which took effect at the start of the 2026–27 academic year on October 1, cover history, geography and civic education. Under the new guidelines, ‘colonisation’ is described as ‘imperialist invasion’, while ‘colonisers’ become ‘invaders’ and European explorers are referred to as ‘spies’. The term ‘ethnic groups’ is also replaced with ‘socio-cultural groups’. The changes go beyond terminology. New history lessons examine African resistance, indigenous knowledge, Burkina Faso’s revolutionary history and the 1791–1804 Haitian Revolution. The curriculum also introduces the history of the Alliance of Sahel States, formed by Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger. Geography lessons are being revised to remove descriptions such as ‘poor country’, ‘indebted country’

According to the hackers, they managed to steal about 23 terabytes of data, including internal documents, demographic and economic statistics, as well as information on Russian losses in the war against Ukraine. The data obtained enabled the groups to make their own calculations of the number of people killed since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
